title: Stock Futures Slide as U.S. Strikes on Iran Rattle Global Markets
excerpt: Oil prices surge past $90 a barrel and Asian equities tumble after U.S. forces hit Iranian launchers on Larak Island, reigniting fears of a wider Middle East escalation.
body:
• S&P 500 futures fell 0.4% and Nasdaq futures shed 0.5% after U.S. forces struck Iranian launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
  • Brent crude surged 2.8% to $90.60 a barrel while WTI rose 2.5% to $85.50, extending the six-month energy shock from the Middle East conflict.
  • Market-implied odds of a Federal Reserve rate hike in September jumped to 57% after hawkish remarks from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh.
  • Asian equities tumbled across the board, with Japan's Nikkei losing 1.6% and South Korea's KOSPI falling 2.2%.

U.S. stock futures fell Sunday night after American forces struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz, triggering retaliatory strikes by Iran on two U.S. air bases in Jordan and sending oil prices sharply higher.

Dow Jones Industrial Average futures traded 85 points lower, or 0.16%. S&P 500 futures slipped 0.4% and Nasdaq 100 futures dropped 0.5%, according to CNBC. The selloff marked an abrupt shift from what had been Wall Street's path to a winning month in August.

A Fresh Escalation in the Gulf

The Larak Island strike was the first known direct American military action against Iran since late July, according to Reuters. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they responded by attacking U.S. positions in Jordan.

President Donald Trump later posted on social media that Kharg Island, Iran's main oil export terminal, was being "blown to smithereens," though the U.S. military did not confirm any such operation.

"Looks like we are in another escalation phase. How long that lasts is impossible to determine. Could be days, could be weeks."

— Tony Sycamore, Market Analyst, IG

The conflict, now six months old, has kept the Strait of Hormuz — through which a fifth of the world's oil flowed before the war erupted in late February — largely constrained. Shipping data showed only five commodity vessels a day transiting the strait over the weekend, and the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations reported a tanker was struck by a projectile Saturday while sailing inbound.

Oil Prices and the Inflation Threat

Brent crude futures climbed 2.8% to $90.60 a barrel while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude rose 2.5% to $85.50, according to Reuters. Oil prices have averaged roughly $90 a barrel in 2026, compared with about $70 last year, with the Gulf conflict acting as a persistent floor under crude.

The energy shock is complicating the Federal Reserve's calculus on inflation. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh emphasized at Jackson Hole on Friday that the central bank still had "work to do" to control inflation, and markets responded by lifting the probability of a September rate hike to 57%, up from 35% before the speech.

"We continue to expect that a hike won't come until December, though agree that the September meeting is live."

— Michael Feroli, Chief U.S. Economist, JPMorgan

Two-year Treasury yields held at 4.34% after jumping nearly 12 basis points on Friday. Thirty-year bond yields steadied at 5.21%, with investors drawing some comfort from Warsh's emphasis on fighting inflation.

Damage Across Asian Markets

The combination of rising oil prices and elevated bond yields hammered Asian equities in Monday trading. Japan's Nikkei fell 1.6%, South Korea's market dropped 2.2%, and MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan lost 1.2%, according to Reuters.

Chinese blue chips eased 0.7%, weighed down by a manufacturing PMI reading of 49.8 in August — better than July's 49.2 but still below the threshold signaling expansion.

European futures also pointed lower, with EUROSTOXX 50 futures down 0.5% and DAX futures off 0.4%.

What Comes Next

The key data point for the week is Friday's August payrolls report. Economists forecast a gain of 58,000 jobs following July's shock decline of 23,000, with unemployment expected to hold at 4.1%. A weaker-than-expected report could ease pressure on the Fed to hike as early as September, while a strong reading would reinforce the hawkish stance.

Gold fell 1.0% to $4,405 an ounce as rising yields dimmed the appeal of the non-yielding metal. The dollar edged lower against the yen at 159.78 but remained well above levels that would trigger intervention concerns.

G20 finance ministers and central bankers meet in North Carolina on Monday and Tuesday, where inflation, interest rates, and the economic fallout from the Gulf conflict are expected to dominate discussions. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Reuters he planned to meet with the Bank of Japan's head amid growing speculation of a Japanese rate hike in September.
image_caption: The Strait of Hormuz, where U.S. forces struck Iranian launchers on Larak Island. The military escalation sent global stock futures sliding and crude oil prices surging.
nri_angle: Rising oil prices and potential Fed rate hikes could increase inflationary pressure on U.S. households, including the Indian diaspora.
